Compounding

Can't swallow pills? Liquids, troches, rapid-dissolve tablets and gels.

Lots of people, from young kids to older parents, struggle with pills. Before you crush or split one, here's what's safe, what other forms exist, and how to ask your prescriber for one.

Reviewed by Ian Tasman, PharmD, owner and pharmacist · Updated November 25, 2026

Why pills are hard for some people

Trouble swallowing pills is more common than most people think. It can come from:

  • Age. Young children often can't swallow tablets yet, and swallowing can get harder with age.
  • Medical conditions such as stroke, Parkinson's disease, dementia, dry mouth, or treatment for head and neck cancer.
  • A strong gag reflex or anxiety about pills, even in healthy adults.
  • Pill size or number. Large tablets, or many medicines a day, wear people down.
Tell your doctor about new swallowing trouble. Coughing or choking when you eat or drink, food or pills that feel stuck, or pain when swallowing can be signs of a medical problem that needs checking. Get emergency care right away if something is stuck and you can't breathe or swallow your saliva.

Why crushing or splitting isn't always safe

Many tablets can be crushed or split, but some must not be. Changing them can be dangerous or make them stop working:

  • Extended-release tablets and capsules (often marked ER, XR, XL, SR or CR) are built to release medicine slowly. Crushing them can release a whole day's dose at once.
  • Enteric-coated tablets have a coating that protects the medicine from stomach acid, or protects your stomach from the medicine.
  • Some medicines are hazardous to handle as a powder, for you or a caregiver.
  • Some taste terrible or numb the mouth once crushed, which can make the next dose even harder.

Mixing a crushed pill into food can also cause problems if the person doesn't finish it, or if that food affects how the medicine works. Always ask a pharmacist before you crush, split, or open a capsule.

Other forms a compounding pharmacy can make

Sometimes the medicine you need already comes in an easier commercial form, and we'll check that first. When it doesn't, a compounding pharmacy can often prepare it in another form from your prescriber's prescription:

  • Flavored liquids. Measured with an oral syringe, so doses are accurate. Good for children and anyone who can swallow liquids safely. Flavors include wild cherry, grape, raspberry, banana and marshmallow, depending on the medicine.
  • Troches. Soft, flavored lozenges that dissolve slowly between the cheek and gum.
  • Rapid-dissolve tablets. Small tablets that melt under the tongue in moments, often flavored.
  • Transdermal gels and creams. Rubbed into the skin, for certain medicines that absorb well that way. Not every medicine works through the skin, so this option is more limited.
  • Smaller capsules or custom strengths, so a large tablet can become something easier, or several pills fewer.

Not every medication can be made in every form. A pharmacist will check what's possible for your medicine and talk with your prescriber if needed.

How to ask your prescriber

  1. Tell your prescriber that swallowing pills is a problem, and which medicines are hardest.
  2. Mention the form you'd prefer, such as a liquid or a rapid-dissolve tablet. You can ask us first which forms are possible.
  3. Ask them to send the prescription to a compounding pharmacy, or have their office call us to talk it through with a pharmacist.

What happens once they send it

You don't need to call us after your prescriber sends it; we call you. A pharmacist reviews the prescription, we confirm the price with you, and most compounds are ready the same day or within 24 hours. We label each one with storage directions and a beyond-use date. Some liquids need refrigeration. Pick up in Oviedo, or we ship to Florida, Maine and Colorado.

Common questions

Will a liquid or troche work as well as the pill?

It contains the active ingredient at the strength your prescriber orders. Compounded medications are not FDA-approved, so ask your prescriber whether a compounded form is right for you.

Does insurance cover compounded forms?

It depends on your plan, and many plans don't cover compounded medications. We'll tell you the price before we make it.

Can you make a liquid for my child's medicine?

Often, yes, from your pediatrician's prescription. Call us and a pharmacist will check whether your child's medicine can be made as a flavored liquid.

This article is general information and not medical advice. Compounded medications are not FDA-approved and are not commercially manufactured products. Your prescriber decides what's right for you.
